NOTE: the Supplier's position is that this is not a vulnerability.

items.title: Console Connect:
items.summary: UK Region Support: Expanded regional availability to include the UK Region. Updated Favicon: Console Connect favicon now reflects the new Nerdio logo.

items.title: ControlUp
items.summary: Integration is Now End of Maintenance (EOM): Nerdio's integration with ControlUp will no longer be developed moving forward. Starting with this release, the ControlUp integration settings have been removed for new installations of Nerdio Manager and for any existing deployments where the integration is not configured. Existing deployments where the integration is configured are unaffected, and Nerdio will continue to support the integration, including critical bugfixes.

items.title: AVD Hybrid on Nutanix: Desktop image management support is now available!
Device & App Management:
items.summary: Intune & Windows 365: Error when editing Windows 365 items in US Government tenants: Resolved an issue where the error Could not find a property named 'userExperienceType' may be displayed. The user experience type function is not supported by government tenants. This error has been suppressed. Intune User Experience call optimizations: The app service option IntuneUxHistory:Enabled may be added with a value of false to fully disable the user experience history data if desired. Unified App Management: Error when deploying Winget applications which contain unexpected version characters: Resolved an issue where the error No newer package versions are available from the configured sources may be returned during deployment if the application version contains the characters < or >. In this scenario, the source and target version are now treated as identical and no action is taken.

items.title: New Menu & All Features Page:
items.summary: Introduced a cleaner, more intuitive three-tier navigational menu. While off by default, users can enable it via the New Menu toggle in the top-left corner. A new All Features page provides a centralized, searchable view of every feature available within Nerdio Manager, and is only accessible when the new menu is enabled.

items.title: Localization Support:
items.summary: Nerdio Manager is now localized for Japanese. Users can select their desired supported language by clicking on their display name in the upper-right corner. Support for additional languages is coming soon!

items.title: Intune Policy Studio (Public Preview):
items.summary: Introduced a new Policy Studio feature that takes Nerdio Manager's Intune policy management capabilities to the next level with two key capabilities: Settings Explorer surfaces Intune policies alongside their settings and assigned values, with real-time search across policy names, settings, and values. Policy Results shows in-scope policies for a selected device or group, with conflict and duplication flags surfaced inline. Note Device configuration policies are supported with this initial release, however some settings may be unavailable. Support for additional Intune policy types is planned.

items.title: Intune Script Management:
items.summary: The same editing, versioning, back-up, and recovery capabilities that Nerdio Manager offers for Intune policies are now available for Intune platform scripts!

items.title: AVD Hybrid Support on Nutanix AHV is now Public Preview!
items.summary: New features included in this release: Re-image and re-size of session hosts App Attach support Unified Application Management (UAM) support Scripted Actions support Session Time Limits support Custom Views support Please see our AVD Hybrid KB for more details.

items.title: End of Support for AVD Classic.
items.summary: Nerdio Manager for Enterprise 8.0 will be the last version that supports AVD Classic tenants and host pools. Microsoft will retire AVD Classic on September 30, 2026. After this date, regardless of which version of Nerdio Manager is deployed, AVD Classic will no longer function. Customers still using AVD Classic should migrate to AVD using the automated process within Nerdio Manager .

items.title: Settings:
items.summary: Update Azure Runbook Modules: Added the ability to update selected or all Azure Runbook modules to their latest version directly from the Scripted Actions settings page, simplifying module maintenance across your environment. View Egress Path Status: Added an Egress Path status to the Linked Networks settings page that displays the identified method used for routing internet traffic for each network, allowing quick identification of any networks still relying on legacy default outbound access.

items.title: REST API:
items.summary: List Linked Mailboxes and WebHooks : Added new endpoints to retrieve a list of linked mailboxes and a list of linked webhooks. Manage Notifications: Added a new endpoint for managing notifications. Enable/Disable Console Connect Regions: Added new endpoints to enable or disable specific Console Connect regions.

items.title: Installer Now Uses Cert-Based Auth:
items.summary: New installations of Nerdio Manager now use certificate-based authentication for App Registrations by default, replacing client secrets with a more secure authentication method.

items.title: Display UPN:
items.summary: The user's UPN is now displayed beneath the display name in the upper-right corner, making it easier to identify the user context of the current session.

items.title: Azure Files Settings Refresh:
items.summary: The Azure Files settings experience has been redesigned with a tabbed layout, making it easier to navigate and manage configurations.

items.title: FSLogix
items.summary: Reset: Changed the default option selected and added a new option, Archive and delete after 30 days , when modifying existing FSLogix profiles.

items.title: Scripted Sequences:
items.summary: Support for Scripted Actions: Existing Scripted Actions (Windows) may now be added as a task within a Scripted Sequence. Changes to the source script are automatically propagated to the sequence. Cross-Tenant Support: AVD and Intune devices located in linked Intune tenants may now have scripted sequences deployed to them, simplifying the management of Intune devices across a distributed management estate. Note Native Intune applications are not supported with Scripted Sequences. Task Worker Enhancements: Task Worker deployment no longer requires individual scripts and groups per device. Pagination has been added to the Scripted Sequences Executions page and all Task Worker Analytics pages. A tasks tab has been added for Task Worker Analytics , providing extensive reporting on the progress of tasks. A refresh button has been added for Task Worker Analytics , allowing data to be updated on demand.

items.title: Unified App Management:
items.summary: Nutanix Support: AVD Hybrid on Nutanix environments now support the deployment of applications via policies and ad hoc using the session host context menu. ShellApps Cache Efficiency: The ShellApps cache is now cleared on target desktops on a 7-day rolling schedule to avoid potential storage issues. Search by Application IDs: Application IDs can now be searched for and selected when creating application groups.

items.title: Real Time Insights:
items.summary: Auto-update Support for Insights Worker: Nerdio Manager now supports auto-update of the Insights Worker (on-device script that collects and sends data used for Real-Time Insights). As the NME version updates, a backend process will automatically update all endpoints with the latest worker. Configurable Log Directory: Added support for a configurable log data directory.

items.title: Nerdio Modeler Now Supports GPU SKUs:
items.summary: Administrators and prospects can now select a GPU workload type in the Modeler (in-product and online) that surfaces GPU-enabled Azure VM SKUs as the recommended compute options, with contextual guidance on image and driver requirements.

items.title: Intune Insights App Metering (Private Preview):

items.summary: Devices may fail to report the OS and patch versions correctly, resulting in an unknown status being displayed. This is planned for resolution.

items.summary: Azure Files storage accounts with the "Smart" blob access tier set as the default will not appear in Nerdio Manager. We will support this access tier in an upcoming release.

items.summary: Enabling or changing Console Connect regions may result in an error in the 8.0 Public Preview release. Previous versions are not impacted. This will be resolved in the upcoming GA release.

items.summary: The option to move a VM to a different Azure resource group during AVD migration has been removed due to resource group lock conflicts affecting both source and destination groups. This feature is being refactored and will be re-introduced in a future release.

items.title: Citrix DaaS Profiles Flex: Profiles that outlive the desktop
items.summary: A profile stored directly on the machine ties a user's data to a device that may only be temporary, because desktops get reassigned, reimaged, and reprovisioned. That data is documents, application settings, and desktop files, so where it lives is an architectural decision. Security follows the work, so the profile is where security starts: whoever decides where a profile is stored decides who can reach the documents and application data inside it.  Take a user who logs on in the morning to a different desktop than yesterday's. The catalog may have handed them another machine, or IT may have reprovisioned their persistent desktop from an updated image overnight. Either way, their Outlook signature, taskbar layout, regional settings, and desktop files are only there if the profile brings them along.  Slow profile delivery costs every user time at every logon. There's no typical figure for how much, but you can measure it: logon duration monitoring shows profile load as its own phase for every session, next to the user's and the delivery group's seven-day averages. A failed delivery is worse. The user gets a blank desktop, opens a ticket, and rebuilds their settings by hand.  Persistent desktops add a recovery problem. If the profile lives only on the machine's disk, restoring the machine means restoring the profile too, from a snapshot or VM backup that's only as current as the moment it was taken. And because the profile holds documents and application data, its physical location is a data residency question an auditor can ask.  For IT and EUC leaders, that adds up to four questions: who builds the profile store, who sizes it, who monitors it, and where the data physically resides.  Self-hosting a profile store leaves the customer building and owning it The usual answer today is a self-hosted profile store, which the customer builds even when someone else runs the desktops. Citrix DaaS Flex already takes care of compute and scaling and can update a catalog with a new image, though patching the master image is still the customer's job. The profile store adds four more jobs: creating an Azure Storage account and file share, choosing a performance tier, configuring Active Directory Domain Services authentication for the share, and opening a service endpoint from the Flex subnet to the storage account.  Each of these is a place for the deployment to go wrong, and together they split one user experience across two owners. When a logon is slow, the desktop team checks the VDA, and the storage team checks the share. The gap between them belongs to nobody, and the user keeps waiting.  Then someone has to size the share. Profiles grow as caches and local files pile up, with Outlook .ost files and OneDrive sync as the classic examples. A full share stops accepting profile writes, and unless someone built an alert for that, the first warning is a user ticket.  Citrix DaaS Profiles Flex moves the profile store to the Citrix side Citrix DaaS Profiles Flex, as an add-on to Citrix DaaS Flex, takes the store off that list. Citrix builds and hosts it.  DaaS Profiles Flex is built on Citrix Profile Management and gives each user one profile container, a virtual hard disk (VHDX) file with the user's shell folders, roaming application data, the essential parts of AppData\Local, the registry hive, and personalization settings. The container sits in a Citrix-managed user profile store on Azure Files, outside any desktop.   Figure 1. Profile lifecycle: the container attaches at logon, detaches at logoff, and stays in Citrix-managed Azure Files between sessions.  The profile follows the user. Citrix creates the container at first logon. At logoff, it detaches and stays in Azure Files, and at the next logon, it reattaches on whichever machine the catalog hands out. Nobody has to script a copy job.  Logon skips the copy. The session mounts the container where it sits. That removes the network copy, which is what makes file-based roaming slower as profiles grow. There's no published figure for the difference yet, but the profile load phase in logon duration monitoring shows it session by session, before and after the switch.  Persistent desktops get a second recovery option. Citrix DaaS Flex can already snapshot the machines in a static catalog on a schedule and restore a machine, profile included, as it was at snapshot time. With Citrix DaaS Profiles Flex, the profile is never stored on the machine: IT replaces the desktop from the image, and at the next logon, the container attaches with the profile as the user left it. The customer picks whichever option fits.  The customer keeps the decisions, and Citrix runs the storage The customer keeps identity in Active Directory and controls who gets access. Citrix runs a dedicated Azure subscription for each customer, which hosts the catalog's VDAs, the user profile store, and the Azure Files back end. Citrix picks the storage performance tier, encrypts profile data at rest, and protects it in transit.  A built-in estimator sizes the store from each persona's average profile size, and the User Profiles page in Citrix Studio shows its status and capacity, so a filling store shows up before it turns into a ticket. That answers the four questions: Citrix builds and hosts the store, the customer sizes it with the estimator and watches it in Studio, and the region is set once.  Data location is a one-time choice. Citrix Cloud hosts profile data in three regions: United States, European Union, and Asia Pacific South. The network connection chosen when the store is created sets the region, and a catalog only binds to a store in its own region. A company that wants its EU employees' profiles to stay in the EU picks the EU region and leaves any further obligations to its compliance team.  Next step Citrix DaaS Profiles Flex is available for Citrix DaaS Flex for Azure. To see the requirements and create your first user profile store, follow the Citrix DaaS Flex for Azure documentation.

items.title: Post-quantum cryptography architectural considerations
items.summary: Part 6: Side-channel attacks  Sixth in a series on post-quantum cryptography architectural considerations for architects and engineers designing encryption for the pre-quantum era while preparing for post-quantum protection.  Why side-channel attacks matter in the pre-quantum era Post-quantum cryptography is often discussed as a future-facing migration: new algorithms, standards, certificates, and protocols designed to withstand cryptographically relevant quantum computers. But stronger mathematics alone does not make a system secure. Cryptographic implementations can also leak information through the physical and microarchitectural behavior of the platforms that run them. These leaks are known as side channels, and they create risk today.  A side-channel attack does not usually break the algorithm directly. Instead, it observes measurable byproducts of execution, such as timing differences, cache behavior, power consumption, electromagnetic emissions, memory access patterns, branch prediction behavior, or fault responses. If those observations correlate with secret-dependent operations, an attacker may infer sensitive data such as session keys, private keys, or intermediate values. For government systems, the attack can target the implementation, endpoint, smart card, hypervisor, or hardware boundary—not just the network.  Air-gapped environments are not immune. Air gaps reduce network exposure, but they do not eliminate physical proximity, insider threats, supply-chain risk, removable media workflows, shared infrastructure, or compromised devices already inside the enclave. A system can be disconnected from the internet and still leak information through power traces, electromagnetic emanations, microarchitectural contention, or maliciously crafted cryptographic inputs. In high-assurance government environments, side-channel resilience is a core architectural requirement, not a niche implementation detail.  ML-KEM, FO verification and the oracle problem Module-lattice-based key-encapsulation mechanism (ML-KEM), standardized by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in FIPS 203, is a lattice-based key encapsulation mechanism designed to protect key establishment against future quantum adversaries. ML-KEM has three core functions: key generation creates a public encapsulation key and a private decapsulation key, encapsulation uses the public key to create a ciphertext and shared secret, and decapsulation uses the private key to recover the same shared secret from the ciphertext.  To achieve chosen-ciphertext security, ML-KEM relies on a Fujisaki-Okamoto (FO) style transform with implicit rejection. The important implementation idea is verification. During decapsulation, the implementation decrypts the submitted ciphertext to recover an internal message, then re-encrypts or reconstructs the expected ciphertext using that message and the public information. It compares the reconstructed ciphertext with the submitted ciphertext. If the comparison succeeds, the implementation derives the real shared secret. If it fails, the implementation must return a pseudorandom fallback secret rather than expose a visible error.  This verification step is essential for security, but it becomes dangerous if internal behavior leaks. If an attacker can submit chosen ciphertexts and distinguish whether the implementation followed the valid ciphertext path or the implicit rejection path, the implementation can behave like an oracle. The attacker does not need the system to print an error message. The oracle may be inferred from timing differences, power consumption, electromagnetic leakage, cache activity, branch behavior, or other measurable effects. Repeated queries can reveal whether guessed relationships about secret-dependent intermediate values are true, gradually narrowing the private key search space.  Architects should treat FO verification as both a cryptographic safeguard and a sensitive implementation boundary. The comparison must be constant-time. Failure handling must be indistinguishable from success handling. Memory access must avoid secret-dependent patterns. Hardware acceleration must be evaluated for leakage, not only throughput. A correct algorithm implemented with observable differences can still place private keys at risk.  Smart cards and embedded devices increase the stakes Smart cards, hardware tokens, embedded controllers, and secure elements are especially exposed to side-channel analysis because they often perform cryptographic operations in physically measurable environments. Power analysis can correlate current draw with secret-dependent computation. Timing attacks can reveal differences in execution paths or arithmetic operations. Electromagnetic analysis can observe emissions created by switching activity on the device. Fault injection can disturb execution and expose how the implementation handles invalid states.  For government agencies that depend on smart cards for authentication, signing, encryption, or privileged access, this is more than a lab concern. Post-quantum algorithms can have larger keys, larger ciphertexts, and more complex arithmetic than many classical algorithms. Those characteristics may increase pressure on constrained devices and encourage optimization shortcuts. If those shortcuts introduce leakage in ML-KEM decapsulation or related key-management workflows, a quantum-resistant algorithm can still be undermined by a pre-quantum side channel.  Quantum readiness requires platform readiness The rise of quantum computing makes side-channel risk more urgent, not less. Harvest-now, decrypt-later threats already motivate agencies to migrate to quantum-safe key establishment, but migration cannot focus only on algorithms. If attackers recover private keys from implementation leakage before quantum computers become practical, post-quantum protection weakens. The architecture must protect secrets across the full stack: cryptographic libraries, hardware modules, operating systems, hypervisors, firmware, processors, and operational processes.  Platform architecture becomes a strategic security control. Agencies need infrastructure that reduces cross-domain leakage, isolates workloads, applies processor mitigations consistently, and can be updated as new microarchitectural vulnerabilities are discovered. Side-channel defense is not a one-time patch. It is an operational posture.  How XenServer helps mitigate side-channel risk XenServer provides a strong foundation for government workloads because it uses a type 1 hypervisor architecture designed to isolate workloads and enforce separation at the virtualization layer. No platform can eliminate every side channel, but XenServer helps reduce risk by combining architectural isolation with mitigations that address known classes of microarchitectural leakage.  Page table isolation: Page table isolation helps reduce exposure from attacks that rely on speculative access to privileged memory mappings. By limiting what is visible across privilege boundaries, the platform reduces opportunities for speculative execution to infer sensitive data from memory that should not be observable.  Speculative control settings: Modern processors include controls that help manage speculative execution behavior, branch prediction, store bypass behavior, and related risk areas. XenServer can use these controls to help enforce safer transitions between guests, the hypervisor, and privileged execution contexts.  Microcode integration: Side-channel mitigations often depend on processor microcode updates from hardware vendors. XenServer’s security posture includes integrating and operationalizing those updates so mitigations can be applied consistently across supported platforms. This is especially important as new speculative-execution issues are discovered and guidance evolves.  Scheduler adjustments: Scheduling policy matters because side channels often exploit shared execution resources. Hypervisor-level scheduling adjustments can help reduce risky co-residency patterns, manage simultaneous execution contexts, and support stronger separation for sensitive workloads. For agencies operating mixed-trust environments, these controls help build defensible isolation boundaries.  Why government customers should consider migrating to XenServer For government agencies, the move to post-quantum cryptography should not be treated as a cryptographic-library upgrade alone. It is an opportunity to modernize the platform that protects cryptographic operations, identity systems, mission applications, and sensitive workloads. XenServer gives architects a practical way to strengthen the pre-quantum environment while preparing for post-quantum adoption.  Migrating to XenServer helps agencies put isolation, patchability, and operational security at the center of their post-quantum cryptography roadmap. It supports a defense-in-depth model where quantum-safe algorithms run on infrastructure designed to reduce implementation leakage, manage hardware mitigations, and separate high-value workloads from lower-trust execution contexts. That matters today, before quantum computers can break current public-key systems at scale.  Citrix is not waiting for post-quantum protection Post-quantum readiness is not a distant milestone. It is a sequence of decisions agencies are making now: which algorithms to adopt, which certificates to issue, which protocols to modernize, which workloads to prioritize, and which platforms to trust. Side-channel attacks remind us that the transition is not only about surviving a future quantum adversary. It is also about protecting secrets from today’s implementation attacks.  Citrix is not waiting for post-quantum protection. We are here for customers in the pre-quantum era, helping them strengthen the infrastructure, isolation, and operational controls that make quantum-safe cryptography meaningful. XenServer is part of that commitment. It gives government architects a path to reduce side-channel risk today while building the platform foundation for tomorrow’s cryptographic transition.

items.title: Security updates for NetScaler ADC, NetScaler Gateway, and NetScaler Console
items.summary: Citrix has published Security Bulletins regarding customer-managed NetScaler ADC, NetScaler Gateway, and NetScaler Console. Customers should review the applicable bulletins and update their deployments to the builds containing the fixes.  Several issues are being addressed in this software release. For details on the issues, affected versions, fixed builds, and any additional required actions, please refer to the applicable security bulletin(s).  NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway Security Bulletin  NetScaler Console Security Bulletin  Recommended action We strongly recommend updating NetScaler, NetScaler Gateway, and NetScaler Console to the applicable builds containing the fixes, as identified in the security bulletin(s).   Cloud services have been upgraded All Citrix-managed cloud services covered by this release (i.e., Secure Private Access, Gateway Service, Adaptive Auth and NetScaler Console Service) have been upgraded with the necessary security updates.  Our Security Release and Disclosure approach The Cloud Software Group Security Release and Disclosure Policy outlines our security release cadence, out-of-band release criteria, and vulnerability disclosure practices. Standard security updates follow a scheduled monthly cadence, with release dates published in advance; those dates are target dates and may change.  Strengthening product security As part of our commitment to continuously improving product security, Cloud Software Group has expanded its secure development lifecycle by integrating advanced, AI-assisted code analysis to proactively identify and remediate potential vulnerabilities. The security updates included in this release reflect these deeper reviews across our codebase, enabling our teams to uncover vulnerabilities and harden the products ahead of emerging threats.  Frequently asked questions FAQ 1: How can I determine if my NetScaler deployments meet the pre-conditions published in these Security Bulletins?  Answer: Please refer to the respective Security bulletins for each of the NetScaler products and the respective CVE IDs for the pre-conditions. However, Citrix strongly recommends upgrading to a version listed in the respective security bulletins for NetScaler, NetScaler Gateway and NetScaler Console.  FAQ 2: Is Citrix releasing any IoCs (Indicators of Compromise)?   Answer: No, Citrix is not releasing any IoCs for the announced vulnerabilities. As of the publication of this blog, Citrix is not aware of any unmitigated exploits for any of the announced vulnerabilities. Hence, there are no IoCs being released.  FAQ 3: I have reviewed the security bulletins and none of the pre-conditions apply to my NetScaler deployment. Can I choose not to upgrade?  Answer: Citrix strongly recommends upgrading because the released software contains additional security fixes designed to enhance the security posture of NetScaler.  FAQ 4: Will ICA sessions be terminated after upgrading to the new software?  Answer: Yes, existing ICA sessions will be terminated after the upgrade. ICA sessions would need to be initiated again post-upgrade.  FAQ 5: Are there any concerns if I am using a NetScaler Console-based license type (i.e., Pooled / Flexed license) and trying to upgrade NetScaler Console from a non-LAS build (i.e., any Console build published prior to 14.1-51.x) to Console 14.1 74.34 (i.e., NetScaler Console build with 12 Nov CVE fixes), without applying for an extension?  Answer: The LAS enforcement deadline has passed, so the upgrade will be blocked if you move from a non-LAS-compatible NetScaler Console build to Console 14.1 74.34 while still using the legacy file-based license and not having applied an extension. It is important to follow the correct order of steps to ensure the upgrade progresses. Here are the steps you need to follow:  Step 1: Upgrade all your NetScaler ADC instances which are licensed using NetScaler Console to the NetScaler builds containing the fixes for vulnerabilities announced on November 12, 2026 as mentioned in the security bulletin.  Step 2: Please contact your ATS/partner and seek approval for an extension (LAS exception of type license file extension).  Step 3: Follow the documented process detailed in the extension document. The ATS/partner will share the document with you along with the approval for extension.  Step 4: Once the extension approved and applied to NetScaler Console, please upgrade your NetScaler Console to the build containing the fix for vulnerabilities announced on November 12, 2026.   FAQ 6: What’s the order of steps I should follow for upgrading my NetScaler and NetScaler Console environment?  Answer: Here are the steps you need to follow:  Step 1: Please upgrade your NetScaler/NetScaler Gateway deployment   Step 2: Please upgrade NetScaler Console.   FAQ 7: Why does NetScaler Console display different CVE IDs in scan results compared to the Security Bulletin?  Answer: The CVE IDs for 7 CVEs have been revised in the Security Bulletin. NetScaler Console CVE repository may therefore display the previously published CVE IDs until the corresponding update is applied in NS Console. Scan results triggered before this correction may continue to display the older CVE IDs.  The CVE ID mapping is provided below for reference. items.title: NetScaler WAF Signatures Update v188
items.summary: NetScaler has released a new version of its integrated Web App Firewall signatures to help customers mitigate several CVEs with varying CVSS scores.   CVE-2026-111497: Google Brotli is an open-source lossless compression library widely incorporated into web servers, browsers, programming runtimes, and HTTP clients to reduce the size of data transmitted or stored by applications. The Brotli decoder is affected by a buffer overflow vulnerability in c/dec/decode.c, where a crafted Brotli-compressed stream can corrupt adjacent decoder memory. Rated CVSS 9.2 (Critical), the vulnerability affects unpatched releases in the Brotli 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 range. Fixes are available in 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1 depending on the release branch; downstream ecosystems such as .NET also issued emergency updates. An unauthenticated remote attacker who can cause a vulnerable application to decompress malicious Brotli data can corrupt or disclose process memory, crash the application, and potentially execute arbitrary code.    CVE‑2026‑65880: Balbooa Forms is a form-building extension for Joomla that enables websites to create and process public-facing forms and visitor submissions. Balbooa Forms is affected by an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in its form-processing logic, where insecure handling of forms containing the signature field type allows attacker-controlled input to reach executable code paths. Rated CVSS 10.0 (Critical), the vulnerability affects Balbooa Forms versions prior to 2.4.1. Unauthenticated remote attackers can exploit a vulnerable publicly accessible form without user interaction to execute arbitrary code in the web-server context, potentially resulting in complete website and server compromise. items.title: How Do I: Provision a NetScaler VPX on Google Cloud Using Terraform?
items.summary: Terraform is a good fit for deploying NetScaler VPX on Google Cloud. You define the build once, and every environment you create from it comes out the same. Most of the configuration is straightforward, but a few settings are easy to miss at deploy time and hard to fix later.  Here's a common example. If the VPX image is created without the MULTI_IP_SUBNET guest OS feature, everything looks healthy: the instance shows RUNNING, both network interfaces are attached, and the GUI loads. But the VIP never answers, because the second interface can't carry traffic. That feature can only be set when the image is created, so the only fix is to rebuild the appliance.  This article walks through the full build and points out the other settings like that along the way: where the image comes from, IP forwarding on the instance, which interface becomes the NSIP, and whether the management interface is exposed to the internet.  Because the VPX image is no longer published on Google Cloud Marketplace, you'll start by downloading it from citrix.com and staging it in a Cloud Storage bucket. From there, a single terraform apply creates the VIP network, the firewall rules, a NetScaler image with multi-IP support, and the instance. We'll stop once the appliance is running and reachable. Licensing and onboarding to NetScaler Console are covered in the next article. The full lab code can be found in the URL that is listed at the end of this article.    Why does this matter? Standing up a NetScaler is not hard. Standing up the same NetScaler three times is where teams lose days. Environments drift apart over time: dev ends up on a different subnet than staging, a firewall rule opened for testing stays open in production, and nobody can say for sure which image a running appliance was built from.  Putting the build in Terraform fixes three specific things:  The image version is recorded. The archive URL, NSVPX-GCP-14.1-73.49_nc.tar.gz in a bucket you own, is in the repository, not in someone's memory. A rebuild produces the same appliance, and the image no longer depends on a listing that can be withdrawn.  Network exposure is reviewable. The firewall source ranges are three lines in a diff. Opening management to the internet becomes something a reviewer can catch, rather than something discovered in an audit.  Drift is easy to detect. terraform plan on an unchanged directory is the only honest answer to "has anyone touched this?"    Prerequisites Component  Version / requirement  Notes  Terraform  1.15.8  1.2.0+ works  hashicorp/google provider  7.42.0  Pinned in .terraform.lock.hcl  NetScaler VPX image  NSVPX-GCP-14.1-73.49_nc.tar.gz  Downloaded from citrix.com  Google Cloud SDK  Current gcloud  For the bucket upload and checks  GCP machine type  n1-standard-2  Set through machine_type  Google Cloud project  Billing enabled  Compute Engine API on     You also need:  A citrix.com account entitled to download NetScaler VPX for Google Cloud.  A Cloud Storage bucket in the target project to hold the image archive. It stays private; nothing needs public access.  A GCP service account key saved to ~/terraform-sa.json, holding roles/compute.admin and roles/iam.serviceAccountUser on the project, plus roles/storage.objectViewer on the bucket so the image can be built from the archive.  The Compute Engine API (compute.googleapis.com) enabled on the project.  Your workstation's public IP, for the SSH firewall rule.  Enough quota in the target region for one n1-standard-2 instance and two external addresses.  Note: terraform.tfstate records every attribute of every resource this configuration creates. Treat it as sensitive: gitignore it, and move to a GCS backend with encryption before anyone else runs this.     What we are aiming for  By the end of this article you will have the Google Cloud foundation for the lab and a running NetScaler VPX on top of it. The diagram below shows the target topology: nic0 sits on the default network and carries the NSIP for management, with a public address; nic1 sits on the <BASENAME>-vip-network subnet (192.168.42.0/24 in the example) and carries client traffic through a reserved static external IP; and three firewall rules control SSH and HTTP/HTTPS access to each side. Upcoming articles in this series build on this environment, starting with licensing and onboarding to NetScaler Console.      Plan your values These live in terraform.auto.tfvars. <BASENAME> matters most as every resource name in the configuration is derived from it, so pick something short and unique per environment.  Value  Example  What it controls  <PROJECT>  adc-pm-demo  GCP project the resources land in  <BASENAME>  kk-lab  Prefix for every resource name  <REGION> / <ZONE>  europe-west3 / europe-west3-a  Placement  <MACHINE_TYPE>  n1-standard-2  VPX instance size  <BUCKET>  adc-pm-demo-bucket  Bucket holding the image archive  <IMAGE_URL>  https://storage.googleapis.com/<BUCKET>/NSVPX-GCP-14.1-73.49_nc.tar.gz  Archive the VPX image is built from (source_image)  <VIP_CIDR>  192.168.42.0/24  The VIP subnet range  <CONTROLLING_RANGE>  [“<IP_1>/32”, “<IP_2>/32”,  ..]  Who may SSH to the NSIP     Key considerations before you begin 1. The image comes from citrix.com, not the Marketplace. Terraform can't download it for you because the download requires a login and EULA acceptance. Staging the archive in your own bucket is a one-time manual step per build, and the bucket is outside Terraform's state.  2. MULTI_IP_SUBNET cannot be added later. The guest OS feature is a property of the image, not the instance. Without it the second NIC carries no traffic, there is no error anywhere, and the only fix is a rebuild.  3. This configuration exposes management to the internet. The nsip_firewall rule permits 80 and 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 to the instance tags, and nic0 has a public address. That's fine for a lab but not for production. Restrict it before using this configuration in a real environment.  4. BYOL means no throughput license. The image you download from citrix.com is bring-your-own-license (BYOL): the appliance boots and the GUI works, but it will pass almost no traffic until a license is allocated, normally through NetScaler Console. This is expected behavior and doesn't need troubleshooting.  5. The instance does not restart itself. The template sets automatic_restart = false. If Google Cloud stops the VM after a host failure, it stays stopped until someone starts it. That's acceptable for a lab, but set it to true for any instance that handles production traffic.    Building it, step by step Everything below runs on your workstation. The Terraform steps run from 1-deploy_netscaler_gcp, which holds provider.tf, vars.tf, and vpx.tf. The snippets in Steps 4 to 6 are excerpts that show the decisions that matter; the complete configuration also defines the reserved VIP address (google_compute_address.vpx_vip_ip), the vip_firewall and nsip_firewall rules, the automatic_restart setting, and the outputs that terraform output prints. Start from the full folder in the NetScaler Automation Toolkit repository linked at the end of this article rather than assembling the snippets by hand.  Step 1: Authenticate Terraform to GCP Credentials come from a service account key file read at plan time. Terraform reads credentials from a service account key file at plan time. Don't hardcode credentials in the configuration or commit the key file to the repository:  provider "google" {     project     = var.project     region      = var.region     credentials = file("~/terraform-sa.json")   }  Confirm the key is valid and points at the right project before you write any resources:  gcloud auth activate-service-account --key-file=$HOME/terraform-sa.json   gcloud config list project    Step 2: Download the VPX image from citrix.com a) Sign in to citrix.com and open the NetScaler VPX 14.1 for Google Cloud download page:  https://www.citrix.com/downloads/citrix-adc/public-cloud-vpx/netscaler-vpx-14-1-gcp-73-49.html  b) Accept the EULA and download NSVPX-GCP-14.1-73.49_nc.tar.gz. Keep the file name exactly as published, since it records which build you're running.   c) Confirm the file arrived intact before uploading it. Compare the result with the checksum on the download page:  Linux / Unix: sha256sum <PATH/NSVPX-GCP-14.1-73.49_nc.tar.gz>  Windows: Get-FileHash -Path <PATH\NSVPX-GCP-14.1-73.49_nc.tar.gz> -Algorithm SHA256    Step 3: Stage the image in Cloud Storage Compute Engine builds custom images from archives in Cloud Storage, so the file must land in a bucket before Terraform can use it.  a) Run the bucket commands as your own user account, not the service account you activated in Step 1. That account only has read access to the bucket, so creating the bucket or uploading to it will fail. Switch back with gcloud config set account <YOUR_ACCOUNT>, then create a private bucket if you do not already have one:  gcloud storage buckets create gs://<BUCKET> \     --project=<PROJECT> --location=<REGION> --uniform-bucket-level-access  b) Upload the archive, then confirm it is there and the size matches the local file:  gcloud storage cp NSVPX-GCP-14.1-73.49_nc.tar.gz gs://<BUCKET>/   gcloud storage ls -l gs://<BUCKET>/NSVPX-GCP-14.1-73.49_nc.tar.gz    c) Record the image URL in terraform.auto.tfvars. Use the https://storage.googleapis.com/ form, Compute Engine does not accept a gs:// URL here:  source_image = "https://storage.googleapis.com/<BUCKET>/NSVPX-GCP-14.1-73.49_nc.tar.gz"    Step 4: Build the NetScaler image with multi-IP support Get this step right, because the image can't be changed after it's created. Terraform creates a Compute Engine image from the archive at your URL and attaches the MULTI_IP_SUBNET guest OS feature as it does so:  resource "google_compute_image" "vpx_image" {     name   = "${var.basename}-vpx"     family = "citrix"       raw_disk {       source = var.source_image     }       guest_os_features {       type = "MULTI_IP_SUBNET"     }   }    Step 5: Create the VIP network and lock down the firewall Management traffic stays on the default network. Client traffic gets a purpose-built VPC, which keeps the data path separate from everything else in the project.  a) Create the VIP network and subnet. auto_create_subnetworks = false stops GCP from creating subnets automatically, so the network contains only the range you define:  resource "google_compute_network" "vip_network" {     name                    = "${var.basename}-vip-network"     auto_create_subnetworks = false   }     resource "google_compute_subnetwork" "vip_subnet" {     name          = "${var.basename}-vip-subnetwork"     ip_cidr_range = var.vpx_vip_cidr_range     region        = var.region     network       = google_compute_network.vip_network.id   }  b) Restrict SSH to address(es) you control. This rule keeps the appliance shell private. It takes two source ranges, controlling_range1 and controlling_range2, so set both in terraform.auto.tfvars to fixed addresses you own, such as your workstation and a jump host, never to a range your provider assigns dynamically:  resource "google_compute_firewall" "ssh_nsip_firewall" {     name          = "${var.basename}-nsip-ssh-firewall"     network       = "default"     direction     = "INGRESS"     source_ranges = [var.controlling_range1, var.controlling_range2]       allow {       protocol = "tcp"       ports    = ["22"]     }       target_tags = ["http-server", "https-server"]   }  c) Note what the other two rules do. vip_firewall opens 80 and 443 on the VIP network from anywhere, which is correct for a public application. nsip_firewall opens the same ports on the default network from anywhere, which puts the management GUI on the internet. For anything beyond a lab, give it the same treatment as the SSH rule:    source_ranges = [var.controlling_range1, var.controlling_range2]       Step 6: Define the instance template and the VPX GCP builds the appliance in two stages: a template that describes the shape, and an instance created from it.  a) The template sets the machine type, enables IP forwarding, and boots from the image built in Step 4. can_ip_forward = true is required, a NetScaler forwards packets that are not addressed to it, and GCP drops those by default:  resource "google_compute_instance_template" "vpx" {     name           = "${var.basename}-vpx"     region         = var.region     machine_type   = var.machine_type     can_ip_forward = true     tags           = ["http-server", "https-server"]       disk {       auto_delete  = true       boot         = true       source_image = "${var.basename}-vpx"     }     depends_on = [      google_compute_network.vip_network,       google_compute_subnetwork.vip_subnet,      google_compute_image.vpx_image    ]   }  b) The instance attaches nic0 to default for management and nic1 to the VIP subnet, pinning the client-facing address to a reserved static IP. Interface order matters: the VPX treats the first interface as its NSIP:  resource "google_compute_instance_from_template" "vpx-01" {     name                     = "${var.basename}-vpx"     zone                     = var.zone     source_instance_template = google_compute_instance_template.vpx.id       network_interface {       network = "default"       access_config {}     }       network_interface {       network    = "${var.basename}-vip-network"       subnetwork = "${var.basename}-vip-subnetwork"       access_config {         nat_ip = google_compute_address.vpx_vip_ip.address       }     }   }       Step 7: Initialize, plan, and apply a) Initialize and check the configuration is well-formed before you ask GCP for anything:  cd 1-deploy_netscaler_gcp   terraform init   terraform validate  b) Write the plan to a file. Applying a saved plan guarantees you apply exactly what you reviewed:  terraform plan -out=tfplan   c) Apply the saved plan. Building the image from the archive is the slowest part of the run; expect it to take several minutes:  terraform apply tfplan    Verify it worked Four checks, in increasing order of confidence.  The image was built from your archive, with multi-IP support. Confirm the image is ready and carries the guest OS feature:  gcloud compute images describe <BASENAME>-vpx \     --format="value(status,guestOsFeatures)"    # ← should show READY and MULTI_IP_SUBNET  The addresses exist and both interfaces are attached. The configuration emits both addresses, and you need them for everything that follows:  terraform output  In the GCP console, the instance should list nic0 on default and nic1 on the VIP subnetwork, each with an external address.   The appliance is running the build you downloaded. Browse to the management URL from terraform output and log in as nsroot. On Google Cloud the initial password is the VM's instance ID, which you can read with gcloud compute instances describe <BASENAME>-vpx --zone <ZONE> --format="value(id)"; the appliance asks you to change it at first login. Check the build on the dashboard, then SSH to the NSIP public address as nsroot and confirm from the appliance CLI that it learned both subnets:  show ns version     ← should report NS14.1 Build 73.49   show ns ip          ← should list the NSIP on nic0 and an address in the VIP subnet  The configuration is idempotent. Re-run the plan without changing anything. This is the cleanest evidence that your code and your infrastructure agree:  terraform plan      ← should report: No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.    Common mistakes to avoid Mistake  What happens  Fix  Looking for the VPX image on the Marketplace  No current listing to build from  Download from citrix.com and stage it in your bucket  Using a gs:// URL for source_image  Image creation fails  Use https://storage.googleapis.com/<BUCKET>/<FILE>  Omitting can_ip_forward = true  GCP silently drops forwarded packets; the VIP is dead  Set it on the instance template  Committing terraform.tfstate  Infrastructure detail lands in the repository  Gitignore state; move to a GCS backend  Reusing <BASENAME> across environments  Resource name collisions, or a silent apply into the wrong environment  One basename per environment     If something goes wrong a) terraform apply fails while creating google_compute_image.vpx_image. The URL is wrong, uses the gs:// form, or the service account cannot read the bucket. Confirm the object exists at the path in source_image, then grant read access:  gcloud storage ls -l gs://<BUCKET>/NSVPX-GCP-14.1-73.49_nc.tar.gz   gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://<BUCKET> \     --member=serviceAccount:<SA_EMAIL> --role=roles/storage.objectViewer  b) The image builds but the VPX never boots cleanly. The archive is incomplete or is not the Google Cloud package; the download page also lists packages for other platforms. Re-check the checksum from Step 2, re-download the GCP file if it differs, then rebuild the image:  terraform apply -replace="google_compute_image.vpx_image" \     -replace="google_compute_instance_from_template.vpx-01"  c) The VPX is running but the GUI does not load. Either the firewall rule is not matching, or the appliance is still booting; a VPX takes several minutes past the point GCP reports RUNNING. Check the tags line up with target_tags on the rule:  gcloud compute instances describe <BASENAME>-vpx --zone <ZONE> \     --format="value(tags.items)"    # ← must include http-server and https-server  d) The VIP does not answer even though both NICs are attached. The image was created without MULTI_IP_SUBNET. This cannot be repaired in place. Confirm, then rebuild with the command in b):  gcloud compute images describe <BASENAME>-vpx \     --format="value(guestOsFeatures)"    # ← must include MULTI_IP_SUBNET  e) You changed source_image to a new build, but the VPX did not change. The template refers to the image by name, so Terraform replaces the image and leaves the running instance alone. Recreating the instance is what moves it to the new build, and it discards any configuration on the appliance, so back up ns.conf first:  terraform apply -replace="google_compute_instance_from_template.vpx-01"  f) Terraform wants to recreate a resource that already exists. The object was created out of band, so it is absent from state. Import it rather than letting Terraform destroy and recreate a live appliance:  terraform import google_compute_instance_from_template.vpx-01 \     projects/<PROJECT>/zones/<ZONE>/instances/<BASENAME>-vpx  g) You need to back it out. A single destroy removes everything this configuration created:  terraform destroy  This deletes the VPX, the VIP network and subnet, the firewall rules, the reserved external address, and the image. It does not touch the bucket or the archive in it, those were created outside Terraform, so the next build can reuse them. Any configuration made on the appliance goes with the instance, so take a backup of ns.conf first if it has been used.   Where to go next You now have a NetScaler that was created by code from an image you control, and can be rebuilt from an empty project with a handful of commands. The habit that keeps it honest is small: run terraform plan on a schedule and treat an unexpected diff as an incident, not a nuisance.  Three changes make this production-grade. Narrow nsip_firewall so management is not internet-facing, move state to a GCS backend so a second engineer cannot apply over you, and set automatic_restart = true on the instance template so the VPX comes back on its own after a host failure. After that, the natural next step is licensing: deploy a NetScaler Console agent and onboard the instance, which is what turns a running appliance into a managed one.  This article showed how to deploy a NetScaler instance on Google Cloud with Terraform. If you use another cloud or deployment model, start from the equivalent template in the NetScaler Automation Toolkit and adapt the values for your environment. The links below provide more details.  Full Lab Code  NetScaler Automation toolkit repository on GitHub  NetScaler VPX on Google Cloud Platform  Terraform Registry - Google Cloud provider  NetScaler Terraform Modules for Provisioning  The automation journey does not end here; this is only the beginning. In the next Automation How-to article, we will continue exploring how Infrastructure-as-Code can drive operational efficiency across the NetScaler lifecycle.

items.title: Citrix Session Insights Flex: Session visibility without the infrastructure overhead
items.summary: Citrix Session Insights Flex: Session visibility without the infrastructure overhead Citrix administrators have no shortage of monitoring data. Session launches, connection metrics, policy enforcement, and application performance are all well covered. But there's a significant difference between monitoring a session and understanding the activity taking place inside it.  Traditional session telemetry tells us how a session behaves, but it doesn't necessarily tell us what the user did. And that’s not just about security compliance issues, but understanding more about how employees are using apps and services, to optimize, automate, and streamline manual processes.   Session recording helps close that gap but brings its own challenges. There's infrastructure to deploy, storage to manage, recordings to retain, and sensitive information to protect. And recording everything, all the time, isn't necessarily the right answer.   What if you could enable deeper session visibility only where it's needed, for as long as it's needed, without managing the infrastructure behind it? That's what makes Citrix Session Insights Flex different.  Why the Flex part matters Citrix Session Recording is evolving into Citrix Session Insights, expanding the focus from capturing session activity to making that activity more useful for security investigations, compliance, and operational analysis.   Session Insights Flex, planned for preview with Citrix DaaS, introduces a different operational model built around three capabilities.  Citrix manages the infrastructure. While the existing Session Recording service provides centralized management, customers still need to operate recording servers. Session Insights Flex removes that responsibility by delivering recording through a Citrix-managed service, reducing the infrastructure administrators need to deploy and maintain.  Recording becomes selective. Rather than taking an all-or-nothing approach, administrators can target specific users, groups, or personas based on security, compliance, or operational requirements. Recording can be enabled for a particular population and disabled when that visibility is no longer needed.  The service scales with demand. Recording requirements aren't static. Organizations may need broader coverage during compliance reviews or more focused visibility for specific operational initiatives. Flex accommodates changing requirements without requiring customers to size and maintain the underlying recording infrastructure.  Together, these capabilities change how organizations can approach session recording. Instead of treating every new requirement as an infrastructure consideration, administrators can focus on where recording provides the greatest value.  Filling the gap between telemetry and user activity Citrix monitoring and session recording answer different questions.   Infrastructure telemetry helps administrators understand session health, diagnose performance issues, and validate policy enforcement. Session recording provides another kind of evidence: the sequence of user interactions within a session.   That distinction matters most during security investigations.   Security logs can establish authentication events, application access, and policy decisions. They don't always provide enough information to reconstruct activity within an application.   Recorded sessions help fill that gap, allowing investigators to examine user interactions alongside existing audit and monitoring data. Deep inspection takes that visibility further, helping investigators examine the specific actions and sequence of events within a session rather than relying solely on traditional logs.   This doesn't replace SIEM platforms, endpoint security tools, or conventional auditing. It adds visual context that those systems may not capture.  However, capturing the evidence is only half the challenge. Finding relevant activity within hours of recordings can require significant manual effort, even when investigators know which session to examine.  The broader evolution toward Session Insights addresses the need to make recorded activity easier to analyze and use, rather than treating recordings simply as video archives.  Looking beyond security Session-level visibility isn't limited to investigations and compliance.   Traditional monitoring can establish whether an application is performing correctly. It cannot, by itself, explain how users interact with that application, move between systems, or perform repetitive and manual tasks.   Recorded activity offers IT operations teams another perspective, exposing manual processes, repeated interactions, and application workflows that may be candidates for automation.   It's a different approach to process discovery. Instead of relying exclusively on interviews or existing documentation, teams can visually examine how work is performed. It brings the usability lab concept inside the walls of the enterprise.    This is especially relevant for organizations evaluating robotic process automation (RPA) and other workflow automation technologies. Understanding the actual sequence of user interactions can help identify repetitive activities, unnecessary steps, and opportunities to simplify processes before introducing automation.  Session Insights Flex doesn't automate those workflows. It provides the visibility needed to evaluate them, allowing organizations to focus their automation efforts on processes supported by observable activity rather than assumptions.  Keeping control of sensitive session data Removing recording infrastructure from the customer environment doesn't remove the responsibility to protect recorded information.   Session recordings can contain confidential business data, application content, and personally identifiable information. Access, retention, and recording scope all require careful consideration.   Session Insights Flex provides customers with control over recording policies, access, and retention, with support for customer-managed encryption keys.  These controls help organizations align session recording with their existing security and data governance requirements while Citrix manages the underlying service.  Selective recording also supports data minimization by allowing administrators to limit collection to the users and groups that require additional visibility.  For Citrix architects, the focus shifts from maintaining recording servers and associated infrastructure to making deliberate decisions about which sessions to capture, who can review them, and how long that information should remain available. To learn more, visit the upcoming Citrix documentation, view our demo videos on Session Insights Flex and Session Insights Deep Inspection, or contact your Citrix representative.

items.title: Tokenomics: AI token spend control in Citrix SecurSpaces
items.summary: Ask any platform owner what their organization spent on AI last quarter, and they can usually give you a precise number. Ask them which teams spent it, what models they ran, or what value those tokens delivered, and the room goes quiet.  AI token spend has quickly become one of the fastest-growing and least accountable lines in the modern engineering budget. Citrix SecurSpaces fixes this by tagging AI traffic directly at the source with user, project, and workspace metadata. The result? Total visibility into who is using what, and actual accountability for the spend.  Why AI costs outgrew traditional FinOpsEnterprise software costs used to be predictable because they were measurable. Cloud infrastructure went through the same growing pains years ago, spawning the entire discipline of FinOps. AI spending is following the same arc - just at breakneck speed, and without the right tooling in place.  Three main factors make tracking AI spend uniquely difficult:  Consumption isn't provisioned: Unlike servers or software seats, teams don't request tokens through procurement. A single developer prompt-engineering an agent can burn through millions of tokens in a single afternoon.  Usage rarely matches intent: A runaway retry loop, an inflated system prompt, or a massive context window can turn a trivial task into an expensive run. The developer sees a working result; finance sees an unexplained cost spike.  Data is siloed across vendors: Organizations routinely mix tools—GitHub Copilot in the IDE, Claude through a desktop agent, OpenAI in dev setups. Every vendor offers a dashboard, but each dashboard only knows about its own small piece of the pie.  When your CFO asks what caused last week's spending surge, you shouldn't have to spend a week stitching together vendor spreadsheets.  Capping spend isn't the answerWhen costs spike, the first reaction is often to panic and apply hard caps - limit daily budgets, restrict model access, and hope costs drop. But blunt caps are a hammer where you need a scalpel. They can't distinguish between a team shipping high-ROI product features and a team stuck in an infinite test loop.  The root issue isn't the total bill; it's attribution. Without attribution, usage grows unchecked with zero ownership. Finance can't allocate or forecast, so every budget discussion defaults back to arbitrary limits that throttle developer productivity.  With proper attribution, spending turns into a series of intentional business decisions. You can spot high-volume projects, evaluate whether a cheaper model would do the job, and charge costs back to individual team budgets—which changes developer behavior far more effectively than a company memo ever will.  Closing the visibility gapTraditional control points weren't built for AI traffic:  Endpoint & VDI tools see a process opening an outbound TLS connection but have no idea what model or token count is involved.  Network controls see encrypted traffic headed to an AI host, but no cost metadata.  Provider dashboards show token counts but tie them to static API keys rather than individual engineers or project codes.  To bridge this gap, you need a system that captures traffic where user identity is already known, appends that context to every outgoing request, and hands it off to an AI gateway to enforce policy and export metrics.  That is precisely how Citrix SecurSpaces and the AI Gateway work together:   Because attribution happens inside the proxy, the setup remains completely provider-agnostic. Models, pricing, and gateway preferences will inevitably change over time - your underlying visibility infrastructure shouldn't have to.  Choosing an AI gateway Because Citrix SecurSpaces forwards requests with standard HTTP headers, you can pair it with whichever AI Gateway fits your stack:  1. NetScaler AI Gateway (Supported, Enterprise Native)  If you already rely on NetScaler for application delivery, extending it to LLM traffic is the most seamless path. It provides commercial support under your existing Citrix agreement, giving you a single pane of glass for both workspace management and traffic routing.  Token-Aware Rate Limiting: Rate-limit based on actual token consumption (TOKEN_RATE) using the x-user-id header provided by Citrix SecurSpaces, ensuring heavy prompt runs are throttled fairly without blocking light queries.  Built-in Observability: Native tracking for input, output, total tokens, tokens/min, and latency, with direct streaming to Splunk or Prometheus.  2. Agent Router (Open-Source, Flexible)  Formerly known as Envoy AI Gateway, Agent Router is an open-source project under the Agentic AI Foundation. It’s ideal for engineering teams looking for broad provider coverage and hands-on control over custom routing rules (including GitHub Copilot).  What the metadata headers look like Citrix SecurSpaces injects three simple HTTP headers into every outgoing AI request:  Metadata header  Default key Question answered User  x-user-id  Which developer originated the request? Project  x-project-id  Which product or business unit owns the spend? Workspace  x-workspace-id  Which dev environment hosted the session?  (Note: By default, x-project-id uses human-readable project names for easy reporting but can be toggled to numeric IDs if project names are internal or sensitive.)  What you can report on Because Citrix SecurSpaces focuses solely on request attribution and identity injection, it leaves logging and analytics to your AI Gateway. Citrix SecurSpaces tags and forwards requests without storing prompt text or payload contents, preserving code privacy.  Your reporting fidelity depends on the AI Gateway you choose, but a typical production stack provides rich visibility into usage metrics:  Standardized metric export: Open-source options like Agent Router emit OpenTelemetry-compliant Prometheus counters for input, output, and combined tokens - fully labeled by model and provider. NetScaler AI Gateway exports similar token counters, along with per-minute velocity and latency metrics, and streams natively to Splunk or Prometheus.  Pre-built dashboards: Citrix SecurSpaces includes a Grafana dashboard template ready to import. You can filter or slice every panel by model, project_id, or user_id.  Key dashboard metrics: Token Totals: Aggregate breakdown of input (prompt), output (completion), reasoning, and cached tokens.  Consumption Velocity: Real-time token consumption rates per minute across providers.  Performance & Traffic: Total request rates, p95/p99 latency, and average token footprint per query.  Guardrail Enforcement: Rate-limit breach events, highlighting which users or projects hit token throttles.  Cost Allocation Breakdown: Dedicated visual panels showing exact spend distributions by developer, team project, or model choice.  High availability & fail-safe routing:  Citrix SecurSpaces constantly monitors your AI Gateway's health. If an outage occurs, you can set traffic to either Fail-Open (bypassing the gateway to prevent developer downtime at the cost of temporary metrics loss) or Fail-Closed (blocking traffic to ensure unmonitored requests never slip through).  From raw data to predictable budgets Once you have clean attribution data streaming into Grafana or Splunk, you can take four concrete actions:  Shift to fair chargebacks: Share usage visibility with team leads first. After a quarter of established baselines, transition to actual budget chargebacks. Self-policing kicks in fast once teams see their actual impact.  Right-sizing model usage: Developers naturally default to flagship models for every task. Grouping token metrics by model makes it obvious where lighter, cheaper models (or cached prompts) could be routed instead.  Targeted guardrails: Instead of blunt global caps, set token rate limits per project or user. You restrict edge-case runaway loops without disrupting productive engineers.  Data-backed forecasting: Predict the cost of onboarding 50 new developers based on historical, per-user token consumption rather than finger-in-the-wind estimates.  How to get started You don't need to roll this out across your entire enterprise on day one.  Pick your highest-volume AI project.  Set up AI Gateway routing in Citrix SecurSpaces for that specific workspace (configuring the Gateway address, headers, provider endpoints, and health checks).  Observe one week of baseline traffic before setting any rate limits or policies.  Most organizations find surprising insights in their first 7 days, and decisions based on real data are always better than guessing.

items.title: Your users already use AI agents: give them a safe place to run
items.summary: AI agents already run inside your desktop sessions. In Microsoft and LinkedIn 2024 Work Trend Index from , 78% of AI users said they bring their own AI tools to work. The survey covered 31,000 knowledge workers in 31 markets. So the question for an end user computing team is no longer whether to allow secure AI agents. Instead, it is where those agents run, what they can reach, and who pays for them.  Meet Maria. She works in finance and logs on to her Citrix desktop every morning. Her company did the right thing: IT approved an AI assistant and rolled it out to her team. Now it reconciles supplier invoices for her, and it works well.  One morning, a new invoice arrives as a PDF. Hidden in it, in white text no person would notice, is an instruction for the assistant: collect the supplier bank details from the finance drive and send them to an outside address. Then delete the reconciliation log. The assistant reads the invoice as part of its job. Because it runs as Maria, it can open everything she can open and reach every address her session can reach. So it follows the instruction.  Incidents like this are already common. According to McKinsey, 80% of organizations say they have already encountered risky behavior from AI agents, including improper data exposure and access to systems without authorization. McKinsey calls agents "digital insiders": they work inside your systems with real privileges, and they can cause harm by mistake or once compromised.  Maria did nothing wrong, and neither did IT. The assistant had IT's approval. Still, three things happened that nobody can see: data left the company, a file Maria depends on is gone, and the session record shows only Maria at work. Now multiply Maria by every user on your estate, with or without developers. That is the exposure this post addresses. It explains why the session cannot contain it, and where an agent should run instead.  The session was built to deliver apps to a person A virtual desktop does one job extremely well. It delivers applications and data to a person, on any device, under central control. Policies, profiles, and session recording all assume that a person is at the keyboard. That person reads, decides, and clicks at human speed.  An agent breaks that assumption. First, it acts with all of Maria's access, because it runs as Maria. Second, it acts at machine speed, often for minutes without anyone watching. Third, it decides on its own which files to open and which services to call.  The OWASP Gen AI Security Project lists both halves of Maria's problem. Prompt injection is the attack: instructions hidden in content the model reads, even content no person can see. Excessive agency is what turns it into damage: an agent with too many permissions or too much autonomy acts on the bad instruction. Threat researchers at Recorded Future go further: completely securing agents against this kind of manipulation is likely impossible. So the realistic goal is to limit what a tricked agent can reach.  In a session, that limit is Maria herself. Her role gives her the whole finance drive, because she sometimes needs last year's figures. Nobody decided that an AI agent should have the whole drive too. Yet it does, because no rule exists for a machine acting in a person's name. When the agent sends data out or deletes a file, nothing in the session tells the agent apart from Maria.  Today, EUC teams answer with the tools they have. They block AI tools with application control. Alternatively, they allow them and add data loss prevention at the edge. Blocking costs productivity, and users find workarounds. Allowing hands an autonomous process a person's full access. Meanwhile, session controls still see only Maria, because the agent acts as Maria.  You can give users secure AI agents and keep control Most EUC teams believe they face a trade-off. They can block agents and lose the productivity gain. Or they can allow agents and lose sight of what those agents do.  That trade-off exists for one reason: today, the only place an agent can run is the user's own session. As a result, the agent shares the person's identity, files, and network. Any control strict enough for the agent is too strict for the person.  Recorded Future expects the first agentic data breach to come from an overly permissive environment, one that runs on default permission settings. The way out follows a principle EUC teams already know: security follows the work, not the device. So the agent's work moves into a space built for agents. Meanwhile, Maria's access stays exactly where it is. That space needs three controls:  A boundary. The agent works in an isolated space and reaches only the services you allow.  A template. IT decides what the agent starts with: its instructions, its tools, and its model.  Accounting. You can trace every request the agent makes to a user, a project, and a workspace.  McKinsey's playbook makes the same call: deploy agents in self-contained environments with clearly defined network and data access, which also lets you isolate one at once. Each section below maps to one of these three controls.  Citrix already runs agents this way, for developers Developers met this problem first. AI coding agents read source code, run builds, and call internal systems. On a laptop, such an agent inherits the developer's credentials, the whole file system, and open network access.  Citrix SecurSpaces™ already gives these agents a governed place to work. A SecurSpaces workspace is a managed development environment that runs on infrastructure the customer controls. It applies all three controls to any agent inside it. The documentation describes how to run AI coding agents in workspaces:  Boundary. Egress is policy-controlled, so an agent reaches only the destinations the workspace allows. The platform brokers credentials and injects them at runtime, so the agent uses them without holding them. The agent sees the workspace file system, not the developer's machine.  Template. An administrator sets these controls once, in the workspace template. The developer does not opt in and cannot opt out.  Accounting. When AI traffic goes through an AI gateway, SecurSpaces tags each request with the user, project, and workspace it came from. For details, see AI gateway routing.  In short, this is shipping product, used for one of the riskiest kinds of agent work. That matters because the mechanism already works where the stakes are high.  The same three controls work for any agent Nothing in that mechanism is specific to developers. The boundary, the template, and the accounting apply to any process that acts for a person. A finance agent needs them just as much as a coding agent.  Knowledge Worker Agent for Citrix SecurSpaces shows what that looks like for people like Maria. It is an AI agent for teams outside engineering. People use it in a chat in the browser, with no code editor in sight. It reads and writes documents, uses the business tools you connect, and carries out tasks with several steps.  Back to Maria's invoices. This time, she opens the Knowledge Worker Agent from her SecurSpaces workspace. IT has already assigned her team a finance agent, the skills it needs, and the approved connectors. Moreover, it uses the model your organization chose. That can be a commercial provider, or a model you host yourself, even at an air-gapped site.  Now the poisoned invoice arrives again, and the agent may still be fooled. What changes is what a fooled agent can reach. It sees the files in the workspace, not Maria's whole finance drive. When the workspace's network policy lists only approved destinations, the request to the outside address goes nowhere. If the agent deletes a file, the damage stays inside the workspace, away from the shared drive. And because the agent's activity belongs to a workspace, the attempt leaves a trace that points to that workspace, not just to Maria. An administrator can also make the assistant ask Maria before it acts.  On Monday morning, Maria finds the month-end summary already done. A scheduled task prepared it overnight, inside the same boundary. Meanwhile, if your AI traffic goes through a gateway, each request appears under her user, her project, and her workspace.  Here is how the three controls map:  Boundary. The agent runs in Maria's workspace, under the network and data controls SecurSpaces applies to every workspace.  Template. Agents, skills, context, and connectors come from one central configuration repository, assigned per project. Each user receives them when the workspace starts.  Accounting. The AI gateway attributes requests from the Knowledge Worker Agent like any other AI traffic from the workspace.  Knowledge Worker Agent is open source, under the Apache License 2.0, and shows what you can build on SecurSpaces. Your security team can read the source on GitHub before anyone uses it with real data. The product documentation explains how it works.   See how the Knowledge Worker Agent for Citrix Secure Spaces helps business teams use AI with clearer controls and less setup: The desktop and the agent each get the right control Maria stays on her Citrix desktop. Her applications, her profile, and her access do not change. The agent simply works beside her, in a workspace built for agents. Each gets the control that fits it: the desktop governs how a person reaches applications, and the workspace governs what an agent can do.  A simple rule decides where work belongs. If a person needs an application, deliver a desktop. If an agent needs to act, give it a workspace. Most organizations will need both, often for the same user on the same day.  This also keeps your existing investment working. Your session policies, profiles, and access rules stay as they are, because nothing about Maria's desktop changes. In fact, the desktop becomes the natural place to start agent work: Maria can open her workspace from the same session she uses every day. Meanwhile, the agent's actions, data, and costs move into a space your platform team can govern on its own terms. For EUC teams, that means one familiar front door for people, and a separate, governed room for the agents that work for them.  DaaS/VDI and SecurSpaces are not competing answers to the same problem: they answer two different questions for two different needs, and can coexist within the same environment.  Start with one team and one agent You do not need a large program to begin. Instead, start small and learn from real use:  Pick one team whose people already use AI tools, such as finance or legal. They will tell you quickly what works.  Read how it works. Share how the Knowledge Worker Agent works with your security team first, so they can review the boundary before anyone else sees it.  Give that team one agent in one SecurSpaces project, built for their most common task, and add the connectors it needs.  Watch the accounting. After a few weeks, you will know what your users ask agents to do, what it costs, and which data it touches.  Then decide where to go next, based on evidence instead of guesswork.
